Longest solo Earth-orbital flight — 4 days 23 hours, 81 orbits

Vostok 5 set a record that still stands. Valery Bykovsky flew nearly five days alone in orbit — eighty-one laps of the planet — which remains, six decades on, the longest solo spaceflight anyone has ever made. It was an endurance test above all, pushing a single cosmonaut and a small spacecraft far past the day Titov managed, to see whether a person could simply keep going. He could. And Bykovsky wasn't even the headline of his own mission: two days into his flight, Vostok 6 went up carrying the first woman in space, and the world's attention went with her.

Valery Bykovsky's 81-orbit, 4-day-23-hour flight — still the longest solo Earth-orbital mission in history. Launched 1963-06-14 11:59 UTC; flew the second half of his mission alongside Vostok 6 (Tereshkova, launched 2 days later). Bykovsky's planned 8-day duration was shortened due to solar-flare radiation concerns and a slow orbital decay. Landed 1963-06-19 11:06 UTC near Karatal after parachute separation.
Landed near Karatal 1963-06-19 11:06 UTC after 81 orbits.
